evidence.title: Automated De-Identification, Consistent Obfuscation, and Regulatory Grade Validation of 2 Billion Patient Notes
evidence.outcome: Re-identification of patients from de-identified notes in independent red-team audit
evidence.effect: A red team working for 3 months on 790 randomly selected patients could not re-identify any of them; system achieved 99% PHI obfuscation and satisfied HIPAA Expert Determination (<5% PHI prevalence).

commentary.bottom_line: Offline and benchmark studies suggest that current de-identification tools remove most identifiers but miss some categories, and one audit of a deployed system re-identified none of the 790 people it sampled. No study tests reassessing re-identification risk after data linkage, although hazard studies show that people can still be identified from masked notes and from cumulative disclosures.

perspectives.view: Eleven studies test de-identification methods. Only one, a red-team audit of a deployed system, tried to re-identify real people, and it re-identified none of the 790 it sampled. Most others report identifier detection scores on offline or synthetic text, which is a surrogate outcome. No study tests reassessment after linkage. Indirectness and uneven results across identifier types lower certainty to low.

Tools miss identifiers even when summary scores are high. Address recall was 0.5 in one study, 2% of entities were missed in another, and about 4.6% of PII went undetected in a third. In hazard studies, an LLM re-identified 9% of masked notes, and 79.9% of simulated people fell below a k-anonymity of 5 after cumulative disclosure.

De-identification can reduce data usefulness. One facial defacing method lowered downstream segmentation Dice by up to 9% and failed quality checks 14-19% of the time, while another stayed within 3-5% of original accuracy. In a German study, a baseline prompt removed too much text. These results suggest validation should measure retained clinical content as well as privacy.

One study tested de-identification on records from seven low- and middle-income countries. Name F1 ranged from 0.75 for verbal autopsies to 0.94 for another document type. Default tools missed Brazilian identifiers (macro F1 0.270) until they were customized. These results suggest that performance depends on language and document type.

One deployed system satisfied HIPAA Expert Determination. A German project anonymized about 60,000 letters for GDPR compliance. Both suggest that documented, law-specific methods can be carried out. Neither study compared methods, and neither tested whether meeting the legal standard prevents re-identification once datasets are linked.

The one real-world validation used a red team that worked for three months on a sample of 790 people, which gives a sense of the effort an independent audit may require. A model fine-tuned on combined corpora reached strict F1 0.9447, compared with 0.8172 for the best baseline, which suggests off-the-shelf tools may need local adaptation. No study reported costs.

Some patients may face higher risk than others. Pathological speech, especially in adults with dysphonia, showed higher re-identification risk than healthy speech in one study. Psychiatric narratives required a specialized method to reach low identifiability. No study asked patients about their views or measured patient trust.

commentary.research_gap: No study tests whether reassessing re-identification risk after dataset linkage reduces actual re-identification. Only one study used an attack-based validation in a real deployment. No study compared governance processes, such as documented method selection and pre-use validation, against usual practice, and none reported costs or staffing needs.
